@@3848886 <h> SCHNEIDEREIT : Here 's how to make sense of Paris climate talks <p> U.S. President Barack Obama , left , and other world leaders applaud as they pose for a group photo at the United Nations Climate Change Conference outside Paris on Monday . ( JACKY NAEGELEN/AP ) <p> Despite the tankerloads of ink -- and their cyberspace equivalent -- now being spilled on the possibility of a groundbreaking deal to control global warming coming out of the current super summit in Paris , let 's cut to the chase , shall we ? <p> Unless the world falls down the rabbit hole and conducts these talks in Wonderland , the Paris talks -- which wind up Dec. 11 -- wo n't lead to legally binding targets on nations ' greenhouse gas emissions . <p> There 'll likely be targets , all right , called Intended Nationally Determined Contributions ( INDCs ) , but countries will set them themselves and will face no penalties -- beyond global tut-tutting -- if they fail to meet them . <p> By the way , of the 90-some INDCs apparently set @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ couple have been judged sufficient to meet the announced goal of keeping the world 's temperature rise to a maximum of 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels . <p> But I digress . <p> Though hardly alone in this position among the players , the United States ' negotiators -- key to any global deal -- are extremely unlikely to agree to any targets that would be legally binding . <p> The reason is simple . Any such agreement would significantly impact U.S. laws , giving it the status of an international treaty . Under the American constitution , all international treaties signed by the president must be ratified by two-thirds of the U.S. Senate before they can take effect . <p> The likelihood of the current U.S. Senate approving such a treaty are roughly on par with expecting former prime minister Stephen Harper , now an opposition MP representing Calgary Heritage , to jump from the Tories to the Green party . <p> In other words , unthinkable . <p> Current Republican majority control of the U.S. Senate has been blamed for that state of affairs . But let 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ was contemplating signing a legally binding international climate change treaty setting emissions limits . <p> In 1997 , as President Bill Clinton 's administration was involved in talks that would ultimately lead to the first Kyoto protocol , the Senate voted 95 to 0 -- a cross-partisan show of unity by Republicans and Democrats -- to lay out the conditions any climate treaty had to meet to be acceptable . <p> That shot across Clinton 's bow included two key provisions . First , that the treaty could impose no greenhouse gas emission limits on the U.S. unless developing nations also accepted such limits . Second , that the treaty could not result in serious harm to the U.S. economy . <p> The following year , Clinton signed Kyoto , which imposed no emission limits on developing nations . But that was simply for dramatic effect . The president -- knowing the treaty had zero chance of being ratified -- never submitted it to the Senate . The U.S. was never part of Kyoto . <p> President Barack Obama is in a similar position . He knows he ca n't get @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ so a lot of recent U.S. news coverage has explored his workaround -- getting an international " agreement " that the president could sign as an executive order . <p> It 's complicated , but suffice to say that to work , the eventual deal has to be relatively toothless . <p> The world wants the U.S. to be " in " this time , so though there 's been lots of aggressive talk about wanting legally binding targets , it 's unlikely to happen . <p> Many observers are predicting the eventual agreement will only stipulate countries must be transparent about how they 're doing in meeting their own , self-set emissions targets . <p> The other big hurdle is , of course , about money . Developing nations want , at a minimum , $100 billion US a year from richer nations to help them develop renewable energy infrastructure . <p> In the U.S. , Obama pledged $3 billion US to the Green Climate Fund but appears headed for another funding fight with Congress , which has n't approved spending any U.S. taxpayer money on the initiative . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ home , emitting vast clouds of greenhouse gases on the way , those are two key takeaways to look for in any final deal -- what 's legally binding and how much real money 's on the table . <p> Paul Schneidereit is an editorial writer and columnist . <p> To comment or view comments on this article , please LOGIN or SUBSCRIBE 
@@3848888 <h> Come together , right now . <p> Welcome to The Coast 's United Nations Climate Change Conference coverage . Over the next week , several Nova Scotians visiting Paris for the annual summit will be blogging for us on the ground . Our first entry is from the Ecology Action Centre 's Catherine Abreu ( a version of this blog ran on the EAC 's website yesterday ) . ? <p> ? People from across the world have been coming together every year to talk about climate change for a long time . The progress that 's been made in that time is somewhat underwhelming . Yet the meetings continue , every one an exhausting crush of urgency and hope . <p> ? So why has everyone kept at it ? Why are we here ? <p> ? If anthropology taught me anything , it 's that biological determinism -- the idea that we humans are hardwired to behave in certain ways -- is a load of crap . Used to justify every manner of human failing , the concept is a dangerous cop-out and , most @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ environmentalism , countless soliloquies have been penned on the greedy and reckless nature of humanity , destined to consume and pollute our planet . Nothing to be done about it beyond hope we might one day extinguish ourselves . <p> Humans use culture to adapt to our surroundings . Whereas most other species adapt genetically , over generations , we are capable of adapting more quickly as our environment shifts . <p> Cultural evolution makes us nimble and to it we owe our resounding success -- a single human lifetime could never hope to achieve the cumulative technological advancement allowed for by a culture that absorbs and passes on the contributions of countless individuals , for instance. ? <p> We are at the precipice of the most alarming environmental change our species has yet encountered , and we are the cause of it . We need to adapt if we are going to survive , and we have to be quick . <p> We are in serious need of some cultural evolution . <p> And that 's what we 're doing here in Paris . We are participating in the exchange @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . This includes the transfer of knowledge and learnings between cultures . As one of my fav Canadian scientists , Joseph Henrich , says , " It 's better to be social than to be smart . " <p> And we are doing it at a scale that is necessitated by the extent of the challenge and the nature of the globalized , interconnected civilization we live in . This weekend , roughly 600,000 citizens flooded the streets and mountains and lagoons of their homes , united in their cry for justice . <p> In Paris , recent attacks resulted in the ban of mass mobilizations . Guess what ? Parisians and visitors found creative and heartbreakingly tender ways to express themselves . <p> Some 25,000 people gathered in Ottawa to declare that within 35 years , a world run on 100 percent renewables is 100 percent possible . Hundreds were out in Halifax , as well. ? <p> We are coming together everywhere we can to share stories and innovate and urge each other to greatness . Let us hope we rise to the occasion .

@@3849040 <h> Editorial : Narrowing the scope of student politics in SSMU <p> Last Thursday , Nov. 26 , the Students ' Society of McGill University ( SSMU ) held a forum on restructuring the SSMU executive positions . It has been 10 years since the portfolios of executives were laid out in their current form ; in that time , SSMU has grown such that these roles are no longer sustainable . This semester has been marred by the resignations of the vice-president ( VP ) Internal and the general manager , forcing SSMU to focus on internal operations , but restructuring the portfolios alone will only improve one aspect of the body . Given the inner turmoil of this year , now is the time for SSMU to reconsider the political aspect of its mandate in order to be a more focused political body . SSMU should be political insofar as it lobbies for student interests and mobilizes students ; however , it should not allow the political mandate to stretch beyond its bounds as a representative body . <p> Without opening old wounds , it is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ entity . Considerable amounts of work done by SSMU go unseen by the majority of the student body , but political controversy stirs anti-SSMU sentiments and disenchantment , ultimately attracting negative attention . When the " Motion Calling on SSMU to Stand in Solidarity with the People of the Occupied Palestinian Territories " was brought to the Fall 2014 GA , students were , ( and many still are ) , confused about what actually transpired . Though the motion itself was postponed indefinitely , the whole proceeding left a bad taste in many students ' mouths . <p> When it comes to addressing issues that directly impact education , such as austerity and Fall reading week , SSMU 's role is invaluable . The vice-president ( VP ) External works to lead student protests and engage the student body in these concerns . SSMU should spend its time on the issues that it can have an impact on , such as provincial policy and McGill 's investments . It is not that the broader , international issues do not matter and do not warrant student attention ; it is more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and attempting to reflect the values of all students on such hot-button issues is an impossible task . <p> SSMU should spend its time on the issues that it can have an impact on , such as provincial policy and McGill 's investments . It is not that the broader , international issues do not matter and do not warrant student attention ; it is more so that SSMU is at its core a student union , and attempting to reflect the values of all students on such hot-button issues is an impossible task . <p> This year has seen relatively less controversy surrounding SSMU 's political positions . Its " Motion Regarding the Adoption of a Climate Change Policy " went by largely unnoticed , and no motions were brought to the Fall General Assembly ( GA ) . GAs provide a forum for students to raise issues of concern , and then discuss and vote on them ; the executives are not the final arbiters . Nevertheless , SSMU can be more selective , and must be sure to focus on issues that it has an impact on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , but expressing perspectives through the SSMU is not successful unless it is rooted in the McGill experience . Stances that SSMU has taken -- which are distinct from what students vote on in a GA -- against austerity and in favour of divestment are appropriate because they focus inwards and on issues that directly impact student life . <p> With the recent election of Omar El-Sharawy as the new Vice-President ( VP ) Internal , the potential for SSMU to expand its engagement with students can be realized . Such efforts must not only focus on what was left undone by the vacancy in the position earlier this Fall , but also work with students to address loose ends . The political mandate is certainly one of those ; communicating the options that are available in terms of restructuring SSMU , including its mandate , will be essential . <p> Students do not need SSMU to express political perspectives , and SSMU should not be a microphone for any perspective -- there is too much potential for disaffection . One element in the plan will be conserving energy -- and Manitoba Hydro is central to the goal . <p> How Manitobans can be pushed to cut back on consuming energy -- specifically electricity and natural gas -- is a heated debate . Manitoba Hydro , the monopoly seller of hydroelectricity , has come under fire for doing a poor job on conservation and efficiency . There 's little surprise in that , given the inherent conflict for a Crown corporation created to build dams and sell power . <p> That conflict was highlighted by the Public Utilities Board in its report last year on Hydro 's multibillion-dollar capital plans , which include new dams and transmission lines to beef up its capacity to send power to customers , initially in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ once a conservation leader , but now behind many jurisdictions -- does not give what is called " demand-side management " the respect it deserves . It has underspent its DSM budget by more than $35 million since 2012-13 , and the take-up on its Power Smart programs has fallen noticeably short of goals . Going into the PUB hearings , Hydro hiked its conservation targets , but only for the near future . <p> That 's not good enough , said the PUB . <p> Demand-side management is n't just about conservation . It includes looking at alternate sources of energy , such as solar and wind , to meet consumer demand and public policy goals . <p> The PUB concluded only an external , independent agency could set reliable , hard targets to cut energy use . <p> Such bodies exist in the U.S. , where they also aim for greenhouse gas emissions cuts , watch the shifting ground of energy markets and alternative sources . In Vermont , the agency cut two million tonnes of CO2 emissions and saved 297,000 megawatt/hours of energy in 2009-11 . Energy conservation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ off the need for expensive new generation . <p> Manitobans could use such expertise , with targets and performance scrutinized by the PUB . The technology of alternative energies , especially solar power , is changing fast and may become a real option for homeowners . It 's the kind of guidance an external , independent authority could produce . <p> It is also the kind of advice that could mess with Manitoba Hydro 's capital plans , aggressively pushed by the Selinger government and backed by the utility 's own forecasts of how domestic demand for energy will rise . The plan is predicated on annual rate hikes of 3.95 per cent that will double electricity bills by 2032 . With spot export prices so low , why would Hydro want ratepayers to cut back or switch to natural gas for heat ? <p> What 's the NDP government to do ? Tell the PUB thanks , but no thanks , for its advice . Insiders say the province is set to roll out a watered-down version of an energy-planning agency . <p> It will be a subsidiary of Manitoba @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ independent , " led by a board that , while having a government and a Hydro representative , will be guided by outside experts and interested community groups . <p> Such an entity would fall short of the potential a stand-alone energy agency would have to chart Manitoba 's energy future . It may allow Mr. Selinger to dress up Hydro as an environmental leader poised to cut energy demand by 1.5 per cent annually for the next 15 years or so , along with GHG emissions . <p> But a subsidiary will never jeopardize the mothership 's course , so it ca n't put Manitobans ' interests first . Mr. Selinger should go back to the drawing board , and think again . <p> Editorials are the consensus view of the Winnipeg Free Press ' editorial board composed of Catherine Mitchell , David O'Brien , Shannon Sampert , and Paul Samyn . <p> You can comment on most stories on winnipegfreepress.com . @@3849282 <h> ' The torch which illuminates the world ' : Canada , science and democracy <p> If Prime Minister Justin Trudeau is a member of a frequent-flyer program , he 's already reached Super Elite status by now . Nothing says more about the emphasis he puts on Canada 's place in the world than the number of meetings he has attended and bilateral discussions he 's had since the election . <p> The new government 's mandate to lead international efforts in climate change , to develop a North American clean energy and environment agreement , to re-energize our role in international development and culture and education exchange -- they 're all clear signs that international relations and diplomacy are a high priority for this new government and for Canada . <p> In the post-war era , Canada built a solid reputation for wielding positive influence in the world through soft power . We now have an opportunity to reaffirm this role . Canada continues to be valued around the world for our strong traditions of democracy , our concern for the common good , the importance @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and respected public education systems . <p> There is n't a single global challenge or opportunity facing the world today -- from climate change to terrorism , from antibiotic resistance to food security -- that does n't require scientific research for its solution . So science and science-related diplomacy can play a central role in building and strengthening our relationships with other countries and organizations . These activities , collectively referred to as ' science diplomacy ' , can involve formal and informal exchanges of knowledge and talent , collaborative research networks , and the sharing of scientific resources and infrastructure . <p> By making science diplomacy a pillar of Canada 's international strategy , we both reaffirm and strengthen Canada 's important contributions to world affairs . Here 's why . <p> First , the fruits of science have transformed our world , improving the lives of people everywhere . Increases in agricultural productivity , better health through vaccines and antibiotics , improvements in maternal and child health , powerful new ways of communicating -- all these scientific advances , and many more , have benefitted people in both the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ vaccine by the National Microbiology Laboratory in Winnipeg stands out as a recent , stunning example of Canadian research bettering the lives of people everywhere -- a discovery in which all Canadians should take immense pride . There is much more that Canada can contribute to the world through science . <p> Second , science is intrinsically a global activity that transcends language , politics and geography . " Science , " said Louis Pasteur , " knows no country , because knowledge belongs to humanity , and is the torch which illuminates the world . " Science is increasingly carried out by large , international teams of researchers . Because science is ultimately about solving problems -- problems which are both fascinating and exciting , the solutions to which frequently benefit all of humanity -- science brings people together for a common purpose . <p> Science strengthens the case for open , transparent societies . Helping to foster a culture of science in other countries is one of the most effective ( and least paternalistic ) ways in which we can help other countries develop democratic values . <p> Doors @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ trade or diplomacy that otherwise might have been impossible . During the Cold War , the ongoing Pugwash Conferences on nuclear physics in Nova Scotia played a critical role in ensuring that the personal contacts and relationships between scientists in the West and their counterparts in the Soviet Union were not lost . The Pugwash Conferences played a critical role in ensuring that the Iron Curtain was porous . <p> Third , because the culture of science is one of openness and evidence -- of accepting nothing on the basis of authority , superstition or ideology -- science has been a powerful voice against repression , the oxygen fuelling a culture of curiosity and innovation . The story of Galileo is perhaps the most well-known example of science challenging the dogma of the day . But science 's role in helping to support the values of a democratic society continues to this day . <p> Think of the discovery of the relationship between smoking and lung cancer , the identification of HIV as the cause of AIDS , and the link between fossil fuel combustion and climate change . In each @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the cause of evidence and the public interest in the face of political , ideological , commercial and/or religious interests . In so doing , science strengthened the case for open , transparent societies . Helping to foster a culture of science in other countries is one of the most effective ( and least paternalistic ) ways in which we can help other countries develop democratic values . <p> Fourth , today 's pressing challenges require coordinated global research . Global challenges , by their nature , are not unique to any one country . Nor can these challenges be solved by one country . They can only be addressed collectively . <p> Finally , science is key to global trade and economic development . The United States provides a good example of how science diplomacy can contribute to the larger diplomatic landscape . Americans have been quick to appreciate that many developing and developed nations have prioritized science and technology as central to their economic and development strategies . <p> Under former secretary of state Hillary Clinton 's leadership , U.S. foreign policy widened its views about the importance of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ role of science in forging strong connections between nations was undoubtedly influenced by Anne-Marie Slaughter , a professor of politics and international affairs at Princeton and senior policy advisor to Secretary Clinton . Slaughter has argued for the importance of global connectivity and the centrality of connections to global leadership . " In this world , " she said , " the state with the most connections will be the central player ... If power is derived from connectivity , then the focus of leadership should be on making connections to solve shared problems . " <p> In a world in which knowledge , and the technologies that flow from knowledge , has become a major driver of economic well-being , Canadian trade and foreign policies should reflect that new reality . As a nation that aspires to lead as a knowledge economy , Canada must ensure that its embassies and high commissions emphasize science as a way of building relationships and opening doors between local players and those in Canada 's knowledge-based economy . <p> Canada 's domestic investments in science and higher education also should be viewed as an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in thinking would take advantage of , and align with , the significant investments made by successive Canadian governments in science and technology . Young Canadians , like their counterparts elsewhere , are increasingly globally-oriented . They see themselves as world citizens and are looking to their country to forge the global coalitions and partnerships necessary to address the significant challenges the planet faces . They are actively looking for opportunities that match their ideals and aspirations with practical problem-solving . Canada needs to create those opportunities and , in so doing , create a powerful magnet to attract the world 's brightest young people . <p> During the 1950s , Canada carved out a key role as an honest broker , trusted by both sides in the Cold War and in other conflicts . In these efforts , science diplomacy can and should be central to our renewed focus on foreign policy and our role in the world . <p> The views , opinions and positions expressed by all iPolitics columnists and contributors are the author 's alone . @@3853217 <p> In its recent decision in Midwest Properties Ltd. v. Thordarson1 the Ontario Court of Appeal comments on a number of significant issues in environmental litigation . This case comment focuses on the Court 's findings with respect to a property owner 's statutory right of action found in s. 99(2) of the Environmental Protection Act2 and its implications . <p> Our analysis of Midwest with respect to the calculation of damages can be found here and personal liability for damages , including punitive damages , can be found here . <h> The Facts <p> The plaintiff , Midwest , acquired a property in 2007 . Before purchasing the land , it commissioned a Phase I environmental report based on a visual inspection of the property . The consultant reported that a Phase II was not required . <p> Subsequent to its purchase of the land , Midwest became interested in acquiring all or part of an adjoining property owned by the defendant , Thorco Contracting Limited ( " Thorco " ) . After expressing interest in the land , the defendant , Mr. Thordarson , provided Midwest @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ further environmental investigation . Upon further investigation by Midwest 's environmental consultants , extensive petroleum hydrocarbon contamination was discovered on both properties . <p> The evidence at trial revealed that Thorco , which was in the business of servicing petroleum-handling equipment , had been storing waste petroleum hydrocarbons under improper conditions and in excess of amounts approved by the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change ( " MOE " ) for decades . <p> At trial , the trial judge held that the defendants were not liable under any of the causes of action plead , including the private right of action contained in s. 99(2) of the EPA . In particular , the trial judge found that Midwest failed with respect to its claim under s. 99(2) of the EPA because : ( i ) the remedy was unavailable to it , given that the MOE had already ordered the defendants to remediate Midwest 's property ; and , ( ii ) Midwest had not proven that it suffered compensable damages . <p> The Court reversed the trial judge 's decision and found that Midwest was entitled to damages under @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , although it was not necessary to quantify damages under the common law torts.3 The Court awarded Midwest $1.3 million in damages representing the estimated costs to remediate the Midwest property . <h> Interpretation of s. 99(2) of the Act <p> In Midwest , the Court considers liability as against the defendants in the context of a claim under section 99(2) of the EPA . This provision provides a right of compensation for , among other things , loss or damage incurred as a direct result of the spill of a pollutant that causes or is likely to cause an adverse effect from the owner of the pollutant and the person having control of the pollutant . <p> In its decision , the Court makes clear that this provision should be construed expansively and interpreted purposively . The Court emphasized that it is not the role of the courts to " thwart the will of the Legislature by imposing additional requirements for compensation that are not contained in the statute . " 4 <p> Noting there was very little case law interpreting s. 99(2) of the EPA , the Court provides @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reference to the legislative context and background of Part X of the Act ( which contains s. 99(2) ) . The Court ultimately concludes that the legislative objective of establishing this distinct ground of liability for polluters was to provide a remedy " designed to overcome the inherent limitations in the common law " .5 <h> Recovery of Damages Under s. 99(2) <p> In finding the trial judge erred in dismissing Midwest 's claim under s. 99(2) of the EPA , the Court provides commentary with respect to the recovery of damages under this section in three respects . <p> First , the Court highlighted that it would be : <p> a remarkable result if legislation enacted to provide a new statutory cause of action to innocent parties who have suffered contamination of their property did not permit the party to recover the costs of remediating their property , given the EPA 's broad and important goals of protecting and restoring the natural environment.6 <p> The Court found that awarding restoration cost as opposed to diminution in property value under s. 99(2) to be " more consistent with the objectives of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Second , the Court held that the establishment of an actionable nuisance was not necessary to succeed in a claim under s. 99(2) . Instead , the Court characterized the statutory right of action under s. 99(2) as a " new and powerful tool " that recognizes the inherent limitations of the common law torts of nuisance and negligence . Thus , issues such as intent , fault , duty of care and foreseeability , which might otherwise bar recovery in the circumstances , are eliminated from the analysis in a s. 99(2) claim . As a result , the right of action imposes strict liability on polluters by focusing only on the issues of who owns and controls the pollutant . <p> Third , the Court emphasized the defendants could not shield themselves from the full extent of damages incurred by Midwest on the grounds that Midwest could not establish the property was clean at the time of purchase . The Court found there was no requirement under the EPA for Midwest to identify the level of contamination present on the property before and after the purchase . Accordingly , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ avoided on this basis . <p> Notably , in dismissing the trial judge 's concerns about double recovery , the Court found that the language of s. 99(2) did not preclude recovery of remediation costs where an MOE order had been issued against the defendants . Interestingly , the MOE ( who intervened in the appeal solely with respect to the double recovery issue ) agreed that it would be forced to " redirect " its remediation order in the event that the defendants were ordered to pay remediation damages to Midwest . The Court noted that in doing so the potential for double recovery was eliminated . <h> Take Away Points <p> The Midwest decision is likely to spark an explosion of s. 99(2) claims in civil actions due to the Court of Appeal 's expansive interpretation of the statutory right of action it affords and the scope of damages that are recoverable under the section . Among other things , Midwest signals to plaintiffs in civil actions that grounding an environmental claim in the typical common law causes of action is no longer necessary if the requirements of a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ benefits of utilizing s. 99(2) of the Act as a vehicle to recover damages , the decision ( and the submissions of the MOE ) suggest that recovery of damages for the cost of remediation under this provision may come at a price . In particular , where an MOE order was already issued against a defendant in a civil action , recovery in the action could result in the issuance of the MOE order against the plaintiff to avoid the potential for double recovery . The resulting exposure to liability in the event of non-compliance with the MOE order presents an unwelcome shadow over what otherwise appears to be a powerful tool for recovery . <p> Footnotes <p> 1 . 2015 ONCA 819 Midwest . <p> 2 . " It 's extremely difficult to change people 's minds on climate change , in part because they are entrenched in their views . "

@@3857160 <h> Background <p> This case stems from the remediation of portions of James Island that were contaminated with lead , mercury , TNT , DNT , and other hazardous substances ( the " hazardous substances " ) due to the manufacture of explosives on the island from 1913 to 1985 . <p> PPG Architectural Coatings Canada Inc . ( " PPG " ) , formerly known as ICI Canada Inc . ( " ICI " ) , owned James Island from 1954 to 1988 and undertook remediation of part of the island from 1986 to 1988 . At the time there were no legislated standards for contaminants in British Columbia , so ICI and the BC Ministry of Environment and Parks ( the " Ministry " ) agreed on the criteria to apply to its remediation of the hazardous substances . <p> ICI went on to remediate six areas of the island in accordance with the established criteria . Following a review of the remediation conducted by ICI , the Ministry confirmed in a letter that ICI had met the established criteria based on the proposed restricted use @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " perceive any further environmental concerns " ( the " Comfort Letter " ) . ICI subsequently registered a restrictive covenant on title that gave notice to successors in title that portions of the island were used for manufacturing explosives and batching chemicals and there was a risk of contamination . The covenant prohibited the construction of residential premises on several of the areas where remediation was conducted . <p> J.I. Properties Inc . ( " JIP " ) purchased James Island in 1994 and was aware of its historic use , the restrictive covenant , and the ensuing remediation process and reports . JIP also had legal opinions dealing with contamination . <p> In 1997 , the Waste Management Act , RSBC 1996 , c 482 ( the " WMA " ) and the Contaminated Sites Regulation , BC Reg 375/96 ( the " CSR " ) , came into force , and established an entirely new regime for the remediation of contaminated sites , based on the polluter pays principle . The WMA was subsequently replaced in 2003 with the EMA , RSBC 2003 , c 53 . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . JIP remediated portions of James Island from 2004 and 2006 to meet the new standards prescribed by the CSR . Following the remediation JIP applied for and received a certificate of compliance pursuant to the EMA and commenced litigation against ICI in 2009 to recover its remediation costs . JIP subsequently listed the island for sale . <h> Liability for Remediation of Contaminated Sites <p> At trial , ICI tried to avail itself of the " certificate of compliance exemption " 1 to avoid liability for the costs of remediation . It argued the Comfort Letter was the equivalent of a certificate of compliance . The court held that the Comfort Letter did not meet the statutory definition of a " certificate of compliance " and there was no express intent in the EMA or the CSR to exempt persons who remediated contaminated sites before the regulatory regime was implemented , accordingly ICI was not exempt from liability . <p> On the appeal , ICI argued the trial judge was wrong and that it fell within the exclusion in section 46(1) ( m ) of the EMA because the Comfort @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> The Court of Appeal upheld the trial judge 's decision on the basis that the Comfort Letter had been supplied prior to the contaminated sites regulatory regime coming into force and did not meet the statutory definition of a certificate of compliance . Further , the Court of Appeal affirmed the trial judge 's finding that the legislation did not provide any immunity or " grandfathering " for those who had undertaken remediation before the current regime or had been given a " comfort letter " by the Ministry . <p> This ruling effectively means comfort letters issued by the Ministry will provide no protection to those who cleaned up contamination before the current regime and no comfort if challenged to those who relied on them for financing and transaction decisions . <h> Quantum and Allocation of the Remediation Costs <p> The trial judgment ultimately imposed 100% of the liability on ICI because JIP was " very much an innocent party " that had not contributed to the contamination . Accordingly , JIP was awarded $4.75 million as compensation for its remediation costs , payable entirely by ICI . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Comfort Letter was not considered a certificate of compliance , it should have been given significant weight in the trial judge 's allocation of remediation costs between the parties . ICI submitted that section 46(1) ( m ) of the EMA embodies a " developer pays " principle which dictates that a current owner is to be responsible for the cost of additional remediation where they are fully informed of past contamination and choose to undertake remediation to change the use of the land for their own benefit . ICI argued that since it had remediated the affected lands to the standards in place at the time , it should be absolved from having to reimburse JIP for the additional remediation . <p> ICI 's position at the appeal was that the trial judge had erred in principle by not allocating any of the remediation costs to JIP and by not properly exercising his discretion to allocate costs between " responsible persons . " In support of this argument , ICI pointed to section 47(9) of the EMA and section 35 of the CSR , which grant discretion to the courts @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fair and just allocation " . ICI argued that the trial judge had failed to consider all equitable defences , as required by the CSR , particularly where ICI had done everything right , met all Ministry requirements and had the Ministry 's confirmation to that effect . <p> The Court of Appeal rejected these arguments and held that the trial judge had properly exercised his discretion . The trial judge had explicitly considered ICI 's " developer pays " argument , but in the absence of evidence that JIP had paid a discount for James Island or that its value had increased after the remediation , he held that there was no basis for the Court to allocate any portion of the remediation costs to JIP . The Court of appeal affirmed this approach . <p> The Court of Appeal also rejected ICI 's argument that the " developer pays " principle applies to apportionment of liability and the allocation of remediation costs . It agreed that paragraph 46(1) ( m ) incorporates a principle of liability such that , if certain conditions are met , a responsible person will @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a defence and does not deal with apportionment of liability or allocation of remediation costs . <p> In discussing these issues , the Court of Appeal commented that the regulatory scheme is not only intended to ensure that a polluter pays , but also to compel the timely remediation of contaminated sites by forcing current owners to remediate as a pre-condition to securing other regulatory approvals . The Court of Appeal agreed with JIP 's argument that one can not raise unfairness as a consideration under the CSR for consequences that are the direct result of the interlocking statutory regime . <p> The Court of Appeal 's decision in JI Properties appears to reject equity and fairness as an allocation tool even though those principles are in the EMA and the CSR . It will likely take particularly egregious facts for a future case to revisit these principles in allocating remediation costs . <h> Limitation Period <p> At trial , the court had to determine the limitation period applicable to cost recovery actions under the EMA that arose prior to the repeal and replacement of the former Limitation Act , RSBC @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The court held that cost recovery actions under the EMA are not based on contract , tort , or statutory duty and therefore , are not governed by the two year limitation in subsection 3(2) of the Limitation Act and the default six year limitation period applied . <p> On the issue of when the cause of action arose , the trial judge held that if any costs of remediation were incurred within the limitation period , all costs were aggregated and recoverable , even those incurred well in the past and outside the limitation period . <p> The Court of Appeal upheld the ruling by the trial judge that a six year limitation period applied . Given that the parties had agreed that the remediation costs here began to be incurred within the six year period before the action was started , the Court of Appeal did not need to deal , and so did not , with the trial judge 's findings about when the cause of action arose . <p> Since these important findings were not disturbed upon appeal and the entire decision was upheld , they remain @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reconsideration and it would be prudent for people incurring remediation costs to commence their recovery action within six years of first incurring such costs . <p> Footnotes <p> 1 . @@3860522 <p> Ad ? le Hurley is the director of Program on Water Issues at the Munk School of Global Affairs <p> The year 2015 was the hottest year on this planet in recorded history . Drought , heat waves and forest fires were all symptoms of rising average temperatures in North America . <p> Temperature records invite Canadians to rethink the importance of groundwater . The resource is extensively used by communities , industries and farmers . It sustains rivers and wetlands , plays a key role in replenishing surface water systems and provides resilience in times of unpredictable weather . <p> The impacts of climate change are highlighting the strategic importance of groundwater in this country . As most Californians appreciate , groundwater , like money in the bank , can sustain societies through lean times of little precipitation . Canadians instinctively understand this . <p> According to a recent Nanos poll , a majority of Canadians not only view the essential resource as a public commons , but want to see this so-called " hidden treasure " carefully mapped , monitored and protected . They oppose @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ need to run their businesses at no cost . <p> Public concern reflects , in part , the public 's dependence on the resource . About 10 million Canadians depend on groundwater for their domestic use . In Ontario alone , nearly 30 per cent of the province 's residents obtain their drinking water from the ground . The nation 's grocery stores would be bare without meat and vegetables sustained by groundwater . These realities help to explain why so many Canadians recognize groundwater as a precious ecological service that keeps rivers , wetlands , municipalities and farming communities in good health . <p> But on the national stage , groundwater remains an undervalued and neglected resource . To date , only 19 of the country 's 30 so-called " key aquifers " have been properly mapped . And this federal project , key to understanding groundwater behaviour , flows , levels and vulnerabilities , likely wo n't be finished for another decade . In the meantime , provinces largely give away this unmapped resource to foreign-owned bitumen miners , multinational water bottlers and water-hungry shale gas fracking companies for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ royalties . <p> In many parts of the country , long-term monitoring of vital aquifers is almost non-existent . The governments of British Columbia and Alberta , for example , permit oil and gas companies to fracture shale in regions where groundwater has n't been properly quantified , contrary to recommendations made by the country 's environment ministers as far back as 2002 . The government of the Northwest Territories is poised to permit fracking in the permafrost , where no groundwater mapping has been done . <p> To date , no regulatory body in Canada has set up a rigorous program to track methane and other contaminants in shallow and deep groundwater in areas of intense hydrocarbon drilling . Yet science shows us that all oil and gas well casings leak over time and that these leaking wells serve as pathways for contaminants that can put groundwater at risk for thousands of years . <p> Energy companies can also legally hide groundwater contamination by giving well owners cash for damages and having them sign non-disclosure agreements . Hundreds of such agreements have been signed in Alberta . <p> At the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on basic groundwater science and reset the annual reporting responsibilities of Natural Resources Canada ( NRCan ) for mapping and monitoring of the country 's aquifers . Enhanced mapping and monitoring is needed to protect and sustain the resource and understand the cumulative impacts of human use and climate change . For this , governments need stable , transparent funding . <p> A recent paper prepared by David McLaughlin , former head of the National Roundtable on the Environment and Economy , recommended that provincial governments charge groundwater users a specific levy or royalty . He argued that this dedicated groundwater levy should be used to fund mapping and monitoring programs run by independent groundwater authorities . It 's time to launch such programs now . <p> But more than funding is needed . There is no point inventorying groundwater if governments continue to allow polluters to cover up contamination and other abuses with non-disclosure agreements . <p> Climate change is breaking temperature records , affecting our water resources and contributing to economic volatility . Investment in the protection of groundwater is a form of national security . Like much in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @

In those eight years , when wage and inflation growth was slow , electricity prices for consumers and small businesses jumped by 70 per cent . <p> In the auditor-general 's view , the government 's process for planning the system " broke down . " Decisions were made on the fly or for political reasons . Nor is this the end of the fiasco . Over the next 18 years , Ontarians will overpay for their electricity by $133 billion . But those who have been hardened by the political discourse in Canada and the United States , where climate change is deprioritized , or even denied , might be taken aback by the clarity of the Merrill Lynch message . ( One U.S. financial journalist felt he needed to say " I want to stress that this is Merrill 's opinion , " as he shared the excerpt with his Facebook friends , including me . ) <p> The Merrill Lynch report , part of a series on " thematic investing , " certainly is n't @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ related to climate change . " <p> The forecast from the Merrill Lynch analysts is for at least $13.5-trillion ( U.S. ) in global low-carbon energy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ estimation , nine main " entry points " for investors to benefit from it , from the expected sectors like energy efficiency , wind and solar , to less obvious or lesser-known spaces like nuclear and " yieldcos , " the dividend-paying offshoots of many of these companies . <p> In all , the Merrill Lynch analysts found 220 companies among the ones their firm regularly covers that have some exposure to climate change solutions . Their exposure ranges from " low " -- the solutions being a non-material factor in the company 's business model -- to " high , " where climate change solutions are core to the business model , perhaps even 100 per cent of sales . <p> But simply appearing on the list is n't a recommendation -- after all , while many have " buy " ratings from the firm , Merrill Lynch is neutral on others , and has " sell " ratings on a few , for a host of factors including company fundamentals and valuation . <p> We 'll reveal the winners -- high-exposure climate change companies , trading on U.S. or @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a moment . Canadian journalist and activist Naomi Klein borrowed a set of that piece of Julius Caesar wisdom when developing the Leap Manifesto , which launched last September . Caesar meant it in the context of adding an extra day every four years , keeping our calendars synced with the seasons . Klein uses it in the context of fighting climate change . <p> Klein , author of This Changes Everything , Avi Lewis , director of the documentary of the same name and their team brought the Leap Manifesto to an audience in Paris in conjunction with the UN climate negotiations ( COP21 ) . <p> " We have political and economic systems that seem wholly incapable of rising to the existential crisis of climate change . Yet rather than change those systems and adapt to that reality so we can safeguard life on earth , we have politicians and corporations who are trying to negotiate with the laws of nature , " Klein said . <p> Currently , negotiators @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , are attempting to hash out a deal that will prevent the earth from warming more than 2 degrees . She is fighting for solutions to a multi , overlapping crisis . " Integrated solutions that will radically bring down climate change while simultaneously building more just economies and democracies based on true equality . " <p> For decades , western society has been told it needs to choose between protecting the environment and the economy , said Klein . The protest is targeted at sending a message demanding climate action to world leaders meeting at the Paris Climate Conference . <p> When it comes to concern about important public issues , citizens are most likely to worry about topics that impact their day-to-day lives . We worry about whether the economy will be strong enough to sustain our jobs and maintain the value of our homes . We care about the quality of the health care we will receive if we get sick , and we express frustration about the state of the roads and bridges we drive on every day . <p> So , when polling firms ask the classic question about " what the most important issue is facing your community , " the environment rarely scores high on the list . In the most recent Probe Research Omnibus survey conducted in September , only three per cent @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ topics of concern such as infrastructure , crime , poverty and health care . National surveys suggest the same thing , which tends to lead to the false conclusion that the environment -- and specifically , the threat of global warming -- is not a priority for Canadians . <p> As the United Nations Climate Conference continues in Paris , there is a great deal of evidence showing Canadians and citizens of other industrialized countries want their governments to make a binding commitment to reducing greenhouse gas emissions ( GHGs ) . Citizens are also willing to dig into their own pockets as part of an effort to cut emissions . This is a major shift , as in the past , high levels of concern about the environment could not be squared with specific proposals to introduce carbon taxes and other methods of encouraging people to emit fewer GHGs . <p> A survey conducted earlier this year by the Environics Institute in partnership with the David Suzuki Foundation found six in 10 Canadians are in favour of Canada joining with other countries to sign an international agreement to reduce emissions @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of pact . <p> What is particularly interesting is support for Canada signing onto a new international agreement on climate change has increased in the past four years . Between September and November 2009 -- when the worldwide economic crisis was deepening and environmental issues were pushed to the back burner -- the proportion of Canadians who wanted the country to join an international climate agreement dropped from 68 per cent to 59 per cent . The figure fell further to a low of 56 per cent in 2011 before increasing to the current mark of 61 per cent . <p> This shows that even though Canadians are still concerned about the economy , they also want to see their federal and provincial governments take action on climate change . Reducing greenhouse gas emissions is not an " either/or " scenario , which it has often been framed as by the former federal Conservative government during the past seven years . <p> Even in the United States -- which never joined the Kyoto Protocol and where Republican politicians in Congress are extremely allergic to the idea of joining an international climate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sign a binding agreement that would force the country to reduce greenhouse gas emissions , according to a New York Times/CBS News poll released this week . <p> This shift in opinion on both sides of the Canada-U.S. border may be in part because citizens are starting to see the social and economic consequences of climate change . For example , the state of California forced communities to cut their water usage last year after years of crippling drought . A Probe Research survey conducted on behalf of the San Diego County Water Authority in March found 62 per cent of residents in that Southern California community were in favour of mandatory water restrictions being imposed on citizens . While California has been forced to take some of the most dramatic and difficult steps to deal with the fallout from climate change , the same thing applies to other areas , including here in Manitoba . <p> Say what you want about the NDP 's management of the province 's treasury , but a major reason Manitoba ended up deep in deficit is because the provincial government has spent -- and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the aftermath of major flooding in 2011 and 2014 . There is a direct economic and social cost to a warming planet that is only going to increase as climate patterns become more erratic and the weather becomes more intense . <p> Citizens seem to understand this and are not instinctively opposed to policies that would give them a nudge toward reducing GHG emissions . In 2008 , former Liberal leader St ? phane Dion 's proposal to introduce a carbon tax was swiftly rebranded by the Conservatives as a " tax on everything " and economic voodoo ( despite the fact in the same year , British Columbia also introduced a provincial carbon tax ) . <p> Today , a majority of Canadians ( 58 per cent ) are in favour of a B.C.-style carbon tax being levied in their own province , according to the Environics Institute survey . Support for a carbon tax , which reached a nadir following Dion 's ill-fated Green Shift policy , has consistently topped the 50 per cent mark since 2011 . <p> Even in oil- and gas-rich Alberta , where new Premier @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ last week , fully one-half of Albertans were in favour of government taxing emissions , as a Pembina Institute/Ekos Research survey found in September . <p> The climate is undoubtedly changing -- and public opinion about what to do about this massive problem is shifting along with it . The other top-of-mind issues for Canadians are directly affected by the reality of a warming planet , and citizens no longer want governments to ignore this greater global challenge . <p> Curtis Brown is vice-president of Probe Research Inc . @@3861071 <h> What demands for recall legislation say about the state of Alberta <p> For many months now , job cuts have been mounting ; now we have an entire oil &amp; gas company joining the roster of victims . Spyglass Resources , long ailing , has gone into receivership . The world is meeting in Paris for the 2015 UN Climate Change Conference where no doubt Alberta will be cast as a convenient villain . The province has finally unveiled its climate change plan , which is a mix of the expected -- carbon taxation -- and the less expected -- a hard cap on oil sands emissions . <p> Understandably , people are looking for a way out . Opposition Wildrose energy critic and MLA Leela Aheer fairly recently introduced a private member 's bill that makes provisions for the recall of members of the legislature . The idea behind recall legislation generally is simple : 1 ) a petition is initiated to call a by-election in a given constituency and 2 ) if the petition crosses a certain threshold of support from eligible constituents , then @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ simply , recall legislation is a do-over . It allows for the possibility of a change of representatives before term expiration . The most dramatic example of a successful recall election was the 2003 California gubernatorial election , where former Governor Schwarzenegger defeated then-Governor Gray Davis in a landslide . In Canada , only BC has provisions for electoral recalls . <p> Recall legislation is a great idea . Alberta , a province governed by the NDP since May , voted overwhelmingly conservative in the federal elections in October . Sufficient popular support for recall provisions could very well exist ; social media agitation for it appears to be picking up steam . But the cards are simply stacked against it . As a preliminary matter , debate is required . Ms. Aheer 's bill is a good place to start . But further debate would be warranted on the details . What should the threshold be ? How should constituencies be defined ? Should it be narrowed only to individual ridings or should the recall apply province-wide ? The proposed bill favours the former , and there are pros and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to debate the matter . After all , the government has to vote on legislation to authorize recall elections . The NDP currently has a majority . If the assumption is that it is so unpopular that it would never survive re-election , there is no reason to think that the government would so endanger itself . Governments are in the business of self-perpetuation , not suicide . And that should underline how unlikely it is that this proposal will gain traction . It is simply so far down the agenda that it will never get the debate necessary to give it form , let alone win the votes necessary to enact it as law . <p> This is why concerned voters ' energy is best directed elsewhere , although voter discontent is certainly a very real issue . <p> After all , the government 's climate change plan is now a known quantity , mostly . Only mostly because the plan had some surprises and also because it leaves some nagging details to be resolved . Everyone expected the $30 per tonne carbon tax , but the hard cap on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ was surprising . Indeed , by all appearances , this measure was adopted by the government of its own accord ; the climate change panel did not make such a recommendation . As it stands , the emissions cap is a performance standard whereby oil sands GhG emissions are capped at 100 megatonnes ( Mt ) per year . Current annual emissions are at 70 Mt . According to an analyst at RBC Dominion Securities , this cap should leave room for around 1 million barrels of additional daily production growth , assuming current emission levels . Optimistically , oil sands growth could be above that if the stated aims of the performance standards are met , i.e. lowered carbon intensity . Truthfully , oil sands are very expensive to develop with fairly long payouts , so the more likely result is a lower rate of growth and capital diverted elsewhere . And because the cap is industry-wide , it is unclear which players will shoulder the responsibility for restraining project growth . <p> Either way , the oil sands -- and Alberta -- will bear a disproportionate amount of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . According to FirstEnergy , while the oil sands account for only 8.5% and 0.15% of Canadian and global GhG emissions , it appears that the diffuse nature of GhG emission sources -- practically every human activity contributes an incremental amount -- means that the world requires a convenient scapegoat . Thus , Albertans are to be singled out and penalized for something in which everyone has had a hand . <p> Add the royalty rate hikes expected next year and the government 's puzzling decision to force poorly-designed workplace regulations on family farms -- without adequate consultation -- and you have a recipe for growing voter anxiety and discontent . Given the government 's propensity to issue soothing reassurances to concerned stakeholders before going ahead with its policies anyway , it should not be shocking that many voters want out . <p> That is why Ms. Aheer 's recall bill is getting so much attention , even if it will never leave the starting gate .

@@3864704 <h> Opinion <h> Saving planet , saving money <p> British Columbia is considering its next steps to fight climate change , and increasing the carbon tax is one of the options on the table . <p> B.C. 's carbon pollution is on the rise . To get back on track to reducing carbon pollution , the government will need to consider new tools ( like clean vehicle standards ) , and strengthen existing tools ( like the carbon tax ) to drive down its emissions . <p> But before sounding the alarm , it 's worth looking at what stronger climate action would mean for B.C. households -- because new research finds climate leadership is better for the bottom line than you might think . <p> Even though the price of energy is expected to go up , the amount British Columbians are spending on energy is expected to fall if the province adopts stronger climate policies . New economic modelling by Navius Research finds that by 2030 , households across B.C. could save roughly $1,000 a year compared to what they spend today on natural gas , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ counterintuitive , but here 's where the savings come from : with stronger climate policies , our homes and vehicles will use less energy . <p> As British Columbians replace old furnaces and cars and trucks , a mix of policies and incentives will ensure they will have cleaner and more affordable options to choose from . Thanks to these more efficient products , within 15 years the average household in the Peace River region stands to save up to $1,200 a year , while a typical Vancouver household would save roughly $900 a year . <p> The graphic accompanying this breaks down how much two average households could save by 2030 . <p> Whereas today most British Columbians burn natural gas to heat their homes , 15 years from now many of those furnaces will be replaced by high-efficiency heat pumps -- electric units that transfer heat from outside your home to warm the air indoors , and work even when it 's much cooler outside . New cars and trucks will be more efficient and there will be more fuel choices -- electricity , biofuels and gasoline will compete @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ( or charge your batteries ) . <p> These changes are already happening today . Thanks to fuel-efficiency requirements and innovative engineering , a new pickup truck can be as much $525 dollars per year cheaper to run than a 2000 model , and driving it produces less carbon pollution . Stronger policies and innovation will continue to drive down pollution and save you money . <p> These are just a few examples of how our energy use in 2030 could be different from today -- everyone 's lifestyle and homes are different , and the opportunities to save will be just as diverse . <p> And of course , the benefits of climate action go beyond the garage . The latest report from Clean Energy Canada , A Clean Economy and Jobs Plan for British Columbia , finds British Columbians will have 270,000 more job prospects in 2025 than today , and easily triple that by 2050 , as the province and the rest of the world cut carbon pollution . B.C. @@3864833 <h> What I did on my winter vacation , or how ' citizen science ' is changing polar travel <p> A visit to frozen tundra may not be everyone 's first choice for a vacation , but as fascination with the earth 's poles increases , so , too , does tourism to these regions . And as climate change transforms the remote landscapes , researchers ' interest has also piqued , though access has n't always been easy , or even possible . <p> Geologist Alex Cowan and photographer Lauren Farmer were working the North Pole circuit as contracted expedition staff when , in early 2015 , they began talking about how they could translate their unique access into added value for tour operators and the scientific community at large . <p> " ( Researchers have ) only got so much money , " Cowan says . " There are only so many ships , there 's only so much time in the academic year . We 're up there four times a summer , and these researchers might get to go once . We saw an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ where it 's not being done already . " <p> Their idea -- one that is catching on -- involved recruiting and training a small staff of citizen scientists from among the ranks of tourists on cruise vessels travelling routinely to these ecologically sensitive locations . <p> You do n't go to Antarctica for the cocktails , you know ? <p> Cowan and Farmer tested the idea over July and August , with four round trips between Murmansk , Russia , and the North Pole with Poseidon Expeditions . Select passengers became the Sea Ice Research Team , and everyone who signed on , from the eight-year-old Czech boy to the 75-year-old retired miner , was tasked with measuring the temperature and salinity of melt ponds in the Arctic Ocean , which helps scientists make accurate models of how fast sea ice is melting . <p> " This project is important because it is a test of amateurs being able to collect good data , " says Cowan of their first foray into citizen science . That trend is good news for tour operators , but also researchers -- and the same goes for the opposite pole . <p> Ecological tour operator Ted Cheeseman travels to the Antarctic Peninsula several times a year , and is helping bring citizen science to the region . He 's been in business for more than two decades , and has seen the effects of global warming first-hand , " Glaciers we used to take people to are now gone , " he says . " We do have an impact when we go there . It 's well-managed and our impact is small , but ... I think there 's a real responsibility to do more than go there and take . " <p> Part of a citizen science working group helping other tour operators integrate similar programs on their vessels , Cheeseman 's own company is collaborating on a March 2016 whale expedition to the Western Antarctic Peninsula , with an explicit science focus . <p> Tourists will track whale movement through photo documentation and researchers will record whale sounds and apply multi-sensor tags to track the animals ' underwater movements . Scientists and citizen scientists alike will share their results in real time . <p> Now that citizen science has been shown to have value , the hope is that more operators will sign on , and that as more tourists head to these sensitive areas , researchers and tour operators will be able to crowdsource science , conscripting vacationers to collect data . <p> It may @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of $20,000 to spend time knee-deep in frigid water measuring saline and temperature profiles with a conductivity meter , but Cheeseman thinks it makes for a more profound visitor experience . <p> Education is part of the package offering on polar adventures to start with , most typically delivered by knowledgeable staff and nighttime informational lectures to bleary-eyed travellers . @@3864862 <h> Overpopulation to blame for climate change : Port Hope resident <p> The recent world climate conference is useful , but regrettably a late and inadequate response to a festering global environmental problem . <p> If all participating nations will live up to the general agreements , it will only slow global warming , it will not reverse it . <p> As early as the 1970s , a university course was given in Montreal titled energy and environment . The course clearly identified some preventive actions countries must take to reduce the unwanted effects of greenhouse gases . What happened since then ? Lots of talk , conferences , posturing and not much more . <p> Developing countries blame the West for the last 100 or so years of over polluting , conveniently forgetting that long before North America , England or Europe was industrialized or heavily populated , the damage began and lasted thousands of years in regions where these countries are now located . <p> The cheap fossil energy and food production resulted in an exponential population growth . Our planet has gone through several major @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in a phase of natural warming . The problem however is that human activity speeds up this process towards a critical tipping point . The increased demand for more energy , food , housing , transportation and consumer products is pushing the environmental degradation in the wrong direction . <p> Food production in itself constitutes large portion of the problem . Even poor arid countries with not much more than sheep herds contribute . The demand for meat , especially beef , weighs heavy in greenhouse gas generation . Rice production , the main food staple for many countries , and the harvesting of CO2-consuming trees add to the greenhouse burden . In Paris the 40,000 participants , who burnt much fossil fuels to get there , talked about a lot of things but so far not one word about the real root cause of our present predicament , which is world human overpopulation.

@@3864894 <h> The United Nations Climate Change conference carries on . <p> ? The agreement that comes out of the Paris climate negotiations will include commitments to cut carbon pollution from both developed and developing countries . In the world of United Nations climate change talks , this is a real big deal . <p> The Kyoto Protocol was the first international agreement that required countries to commit to reducing carbon pollution . It placed the responsibility for reducing emissions on industrialized nations . Developing nations were exempt from mandated reductions . <p> The setup was trying to account for two truths : 1 ) some countries are more responsible for historic climate pollution than others ; 2 ) the same countries generally have more capacity to deal with the problem -- because burning up all those fossil fuels has helped them to industrialize and create wealth -- than those less responsible for the pollution . <p> Basically , it reflects a rough attempt at justice within the global climate change framework . <p> The problem is , the world ca n't get to where it needs to be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ stay out of the equation . How can countries like India , where 300 million people are without access to electricity , industrialize as they need to while acting on climate change ? Britain burned millions of tonnes of coal for well over a century through its industrial revolution . Is it fair to tell India it ca n't do the same ? <p> The Kyoto Protocol also set up an imperfect arrangement that asked rich countries to provide money for climate action in developing nations . How will the Paris agreement ensure that wealthier nations contribute their fair share to climate finance , particularly to help those already suffering the impacts of climate change ? <p> Human beings are pretty preoccupied with fairness . But as we all know , the world is n't fair . <p> This map shows us one face @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has on those with the least responsibility for causing it . The map depicts the global distribution of climate-related deaths . <p> The climate gap exists at the global level and it exists within our own communities . This migration coincided with an influx of refugees from Iraq . @@3868421 <h> Opinion : Solving trade issues is key in addressing climate change <p> Greek Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras ( 2nd-R ) and other delegates attend the inaugural session of the COP 21 United Nations conference on climate change , on November 30 , 2015 at Le Bourget , on the outskirts of the French capital Paris . More than 150 world leaders are meeting under heightened security , for the 21st Session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change ( COP21/CMP11 ) , also known as " Paris 2015 " from November 30 to December 11 . ERIC FEFERBERG / AFP/Getty Images <p> As negotiations are underway at the United Nations Climate Conference in Paris , the debate is increasingly shifting toward the moral imperative for adopting a new climate deal . But the reality remains that the economy matters . Many industrial heavyweights located in jurisdictions with a carbon price , like the aluminum industry in Quebec , face pressures when their competitors are n't subject to similar restrictions . Whether international trade issues are included or left out @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ will succeed , or will fail like the last deal , the Kyoto Protocol . <p> Many factors contributed to the death the Kyoto Protocol , but none was more critical than the failure of governments to align the goals of climate policies with those of free-trade agreements . The difference between the climate and trade regimes is key . In the first case , if a government does n't meet its greenhouse-gas targets , it can pull out of the UN agreement with few consequences beyond a momentary blow to its international credibility . But if a government breaks trade laws , it can be challenged before a tribunal and required to take measures that have economic consequences . <p> The sad truth is that the only years that have seen global greenhouse gases ( GHGs ) trends decline are those coinciding with periods of global economic downturns . This comes as no surprise as , historically , increases in GHGs follow growth in global GDP enabled by our access to cheap fossil fuels : oil , gas and coal . <p> Economic growth generally occurs because of increases in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and trade . While the prices of fossil fuels are determined by international markets , the cost of GHGs are not accounted for , and the consequence is climate change , with the costs falling on everyone . <p> The UN and some governments have worked to bring GHGs into the global economy by developing carbon pricing schemes like carbon taxes or markets . This is the case of Quebec , British Columbia and Alberta , for example . Canada 's Ecofiscal Commission recently argued that governments and businesses in Canada should not perceive carbon pricing as a significant economic threat . But , as they noted , many details missing from their analysis are needed for a more thorough account . So far , the implementation of such schemes has been inconsistent across regions and has had little impact in curbing global GHGs . The result : GHGs associated with global economic growth currently trump any progress made by the combined efforts of existing national and international climate-change policies . <p> To boost the efficiency of carbon pricing schemes , nothing prevents governments from agreeing to implement trade mechanisms , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ costs that carbon pricing imposes on traded goods . However , in practice , few have yet seriously negotiated or implemented such mechanisms . Addressing carbon pricing through trade rules will level the playing field for businesses , help overcome free riders in international climate policies and reduce the risk that heavily emitting industries will relocate to other jurisdictions to avoid regulations . <p> Solving climate change is undoubtedly the greatest challenge of our time . In Paris , negotiators are faced with deciding whether or not climate measures adopted by countries can constitute barriers to international trade . Concerns over the loss of competitiveness of exports sold on international markets may push some countries with economies heavily dependent on fossil fuels , like China and India , to prevent other governments from resorting to any form of unilateral measures against goods and services on grounds related to climate change . Fortunately , existing trade mechanisms and targeted measures designed to support industrial sectors highly exposed to competitive pressures from carbon pricing could help address these concerns . <p> Only by bridging the gap between international free trade and climate deals @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ toward a global low- carbon economy start taking place . <p> Johanne Whitmore is a senior researcher at the Chair in Energy Sector Management at HEC Montr ? al . <p> This article has been updated to remove an editing error . The original version included the phase " the cost of GHGs are not unaccounted for . " That has been corrected to " the cost of GHGs are not accounted for .
